original.title: A cotangent recurrence and a solid of revolution
original.stem_html:
For each non-negative integer \(n\), define

\[I_n=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\cot^n x\,dx.\]
original.question_html:
For each non-negative integer \(n\), define

\[I_n=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\cot^n x\,dx.\]
(a)[5]

Derive a recurrence expressing \(I_{n+2}\) in terms of \(I_n\).

(b)[2]

Find \(I_0\) and \(I_2\) exactly.

(c)[4]

The region under \(y=2\cot^2x\) on this interval is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate a power of cotangent and use \(\csc^2x=1+\cot^2x\).

(b)

Start with the integral of 1.

(c)

The volume uses \(I_4\), not \(I_2\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n+2}=\frac{3^{(n+1)/2}}{n+1}-I_n.\]

(b)

\[I_0=\frac\pi3,\qquad I_2=\sqrt3-\frac\pi3.\]

(c)

\[V=\frac{4\pi^2}{3}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the power:

\[\frac{d}{dx}(\cot^{n+1}x)=-(n+1)\cot^n x\csc^2x=-(n+1)(\cot^n x+\cot^{n+2}x).\]

At the upper limit the power is zero; at the lower limit it is \(3^{(n+1)/2}\). Thus

\[-3^{(n+1)/2}=-(n+1)(I_n+I_{n+2}).\]

Rearrange to obtain the stated recurrence.

(b)

The interval has length \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Put \(n=0\) into the recurrence:

\[I_2=\sqrt3-I_0=\sqrt3-\frac\pi3.\]

(c)

The disc formula requires the square of the ordinate:

\[V=\pi\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}(2\cot^2x)^2\,dx=4\pi I_4.\]
\[I_4=\frac{3^{3/2}}3-I_2=\frac\pi3.\]
\[V=\frac{4\pi^2}3.\]

original.title: Recovering an exponent from a volume
original.stem_html: For \(a\gt 0\), the curve \(y=3(x/2)^a\) is considered on \(0\le x\le2\).
original.question_html:
For \(a\gt 0\), the curve \(y=3(x/2)^a\) is considered on \(0\le x\le2\).

(a)[3]

Find the mean value of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) on this interval.

(b)[3]

The region under the curve is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Its volume is \(6\pi\). Determine \(a\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the integral divided by the interval length.

(b)

Square the function before integrating.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{3}{a+1}\]

(b)

\[a=1\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The interval length is 2. Hence

\[\bar y=\frac12\int_0^2 3(x/2)^a\,dx=\frac32\cdot\frac{2}{a+1}=\frac3{a+1}.\]

(b)

Using discs,

\[V=\pi\int_0^2 9(x/2)^{2a}\,dx=\frac{18\pi}{2a+1}.\]

Equating this to \(6\pi\) gives \(2a+1=3\), so \(a=1\), which satisfies \(a\gt 0\).

parts.solution_html:

\[\bar y=\frac12\int_0^2 3(x/2)^a\,dx=\frac32\cdot\frac{2}{a+1}=\frac3{a+1}.\]
parts.hint_html: Use the integral divided by the interval length.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: The region under the curve is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Its volume is \(6\pi\). Determine \(a\).
parts.solution_html:
Using discs,

\[V=\pi\int_0^2 9(x/2)^{2a}\,dx=\frac{18\pi}{2a+1}.\]

Equating this to \(6\pi\) gives \(2a+1=3\), so \(a=1\), which satisfies \(a\gt 0\).

original.title: A weighted secant integral
original.stem_html:
Let

\[I_n=\int_0^{\pi/6}\sec^n x\tan^2x\,dx\quad(n\ge0).\]
original.question_html:
Let

\[I_n=\int_0^{\pi/6}\sec^n x\tan^2x\,dx\quad(n\ge0).\]
(a)[2]

Use \(u=\tan x\) to find \(I_2\).

(b)[5]

By differentiating \(\sec^{n-2}x\tan^3x\), derive a recurrence linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\) for integers \(n\ge2\).

(c)[3]

Hence find the mean value of \(\sec^6x\tan^2x\) over the same interval.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Transform the limits as well as the integrand.

(b)

Keep the boundary term; it is not zero at \(\frac{\pi}{6}\).

(c)

Use both the n=4 and n=6 cases.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{27}\]

(b)

\[(n+1)I_n=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}\left(\frac2{\sqrt3}\right)^{n-2}+(n-2)I_{n-2}.\]

(c)

\[\frac{304 \sqrt{3}}{945 \pi}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[I_2=\int_0^{1/\sqrt3}u^2\,du=\left[\frac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{27}.\]

(b)

\[\frac{d}{dx}(\sec^{n-2}x\tan^3x)=(n-2)\sec^{n-2}x\tan^4x+3\sec^n x\tan^2x.\]

Replace \(\tan^4x\) by \(\tan^2x(\sec^2x-1)\). The derivative becomes

\[(n+1)\sec^n x\tan^2x-(n-2)\sec^{n-2}x\tan^2x.\]

Integration gives the recurrence; the upper boundary is \((2/\sqrt3)^{n-2}/(3\sqrt3)\) and the lower boundary is zero.

(c)

Successive use of the recurrence gives

\[I_4=\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{45},\qquad I_6=\frac{152 \sqrt{3}}{2835}.\]

Divide the integral by the interval length:

\[\text{mean}=\frac6\pi I_6=\frac{304 \sqrt{3}}{945 \pi}.\]

original.title: A translated circular-root integral
original.question_html:
(a)[5]

Find the exact value of

\[\int_6^8\frac{dx}{\sqrt{12x-x^2-20}}.\]
original.hint_html:
(a)

Find an appropriate substitution, then transform both limits.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\pi}{6}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Complete the square: \(12x-x^2-20=16-(x-6)^2\). Set \(u=(x-6)/4\); the limits become 0 and \(\frac{1}{2}\).

An antiderivative on the stated interval is

\[\sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{4} - \frac{3}{2} \right)}\]

Applying the limits gives

\[\int_{6}^{8} \frac{1}{\sqrt{16 - \left(x - 6\right)^{2}}}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{6}.\]

original.title: An inverse-hyperbolic endpoint integral
original.question_html:
(a)[4]

Evaluate

\[\int_5^7\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x-2)^2-9}},\]

giving a logarithmic exact answer. Treat the lower endpoint as a one-sided limit.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Find an appropriate substitution, then transform both limits.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\ln{\left(3 \right)}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=(x-2)/3\). The integral becomes \(\int_1^{5/3}(u^2-1)^{-1/2}\,du\). At \(u=1\) the integrand is unbounded, but \(\cosh^{-1}u\to0\) as \(u\to1^+\).

\[\cosh^{-1}\frac53=\ln\left(\frac53+\frac43\right)=\ln3.\]

An antiderivative on the stated interval is

\[\cosh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \right)}\]

Applying the limits gives

\[\int_{5}^{7} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 9}}\,dx=\ln{\left(3 \right)}.\]

Thus the requested logarithmic value is \(\ln3\).

original.title: A decaying profile and a volume bisector
original.question_html:
Let \(f(x)=2e^{-3x}\) for \(0\le x\le1\).

(a)[3]

Find the mean value of \(f\,^{\prime}(x)\) on the interval.

(b)[3]

Find the volume generated by rotating the region under \(y=f(x)\) about the \(x\)-axis.

(c)[5]

The plane \(x=c\) divides this solid into two equal volumes. Determine \(c\) exactly and explain why it is unique.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Integrate the derivative rather than its magnitude.

(b)

The volume requires f squared.

(c)

Equate the accumulated volume to half the total.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[-2 + \frac{2}{e^{3}}\]

(b)

\[\frac{2 \pi \left(1 - e^{-6}\right)}{3}\]

(c)

\[- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{1}{2 e^{6}} + \frac{1}{2} \right)}}{6}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The fundamental theorem gives

\[\frac1{1-0}\int_0^1 f\,^{\prime}(x)\,dx=f(1)-f(0)=2(e^{-3}-1).\]

(b)

\[V=\pi\int_0^1 4e^{-6x}\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{3}(1-e^{-6}).\]

(c)

\[\frac{2\pi}{3}(1-e^{-6c})=\frac12\cdot\frac{2\pi}{3}(1-e^{-6}).\]
\[e^{-6c}=\frac{1+e^{-6}}2,\qquad c=\frac16\ln\frac2{1+e^{-6}}.\]

This value lies between 0 and 1. The accumulated volume has derivative \(4\pi e^{-6c}\gt 0\), so it is strictly increasing and the bisecting value is unique.

parts.solution_html:

\[\frac1{1-0}\int_0^1 f\,^{\prime}(x)\,dx=f(1)-f(0)=2(e^{-3}-1).\]

original.title: Averages in two different variables
original.stem_html: The variables satisfy \(y=2e^{3x}\), where \(0\le x\le\frac13\ln2\).
original.question_html:
The variables satisfy \(y=2e^{3x}\), where \(0\le x\le\frac13\ln2\).

(a)[3]

Find the mean value of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).

(b)[3]

Find the mean value of \(x\) with respect to \(y\) over the corresponding \(y\)-interval.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the x-interval length.

(b)

Find the new endpoints before averaging.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{2}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\]

(b)

\[- \frac{1}{3} + \frac{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{3}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\bar y=\frac3{\ln2}\int_0^{(\ln2)/3}2e^{3x}\,dx=\frac3{\ln2}\cdot\frac23=\frac2{\ln2}.\]

(b)

Now \(x=\frac13\ln(y/2)\) and \(2\le y\le4\). Hence

\[\bar x=\frac12\int_2^4\frac13\ln(y/2)\,dy=\frac16[y\ln(y/2)-y]_2^4=\frac{2\ln2-1}3.\]

original.title: Determining a scale from surface area
original.stem_html: The arc \(y=2\sqrt{x+a}\), \(0\le x\le3\), has \(a\gt 0\).
original.question_html:
The arc \(y=2\sqrt{x+a}\), \(0\le x\le3\), has \(a\gt 0\).

(a)[4]

Show that its surface area about the \(x\)-axis is

\[S=\frac{8\pi}{3}\left((a+4)^{3/2}-(a+1)^{3/2}\right).\]
(b)[2]

Verify that \(a=3\) gives \(S=\frac{8\pi}{3}(7\sqrt7-8)\), and show that no other positive \(a\) gives this area.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the two square roots before integrating.

(b)

Differentiate the area with respect to the parameter.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[S=\frac{8\pi}{3}\left((a+4)^{3/2}-(a+1)^{3/2}\right)\]

(b)

The unique value is \(a=3\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The radius is positive and \(y^{\prime}=1/\sqrt{x+a}\). Thus

\[y\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}=2\sqrt{x+a+1}.\]
\[S=4\pi\int_0^3\sqrt{x+a+1}\,dx=\frac{8\pi}{3}[(x+a+1)^{3/2}]_0^3.\]

(b)

Substitution gives the required expression. Also

\[\frac{dS}{da}=4\pi(\sqrt{a+4}-\sqrt{a+1})\gt 0.\]

Therefore the surface area is strictly increasing in \(a\), proving uniqueness.

parts.prompt_html:
Show that its surface area about the \(x\)-axis is

\[S=\frac{8\pi}{3}\left((a+4)^{3/2}-(a+1)^{3/2}\right).\]
parts.solution_html:
The radius is positive and \(y^{\prime}=1/\sqrt{x+a}\). Thus

\[y\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}=2\sqrt{x+a+1}.\]
\[S=4\pi\int_0^3\sqrt{x+a+1}\,dx=\frac{8\pi}{3}[(x+a+1)^{3/2}]_0^3.\]

original.title: An exponential recurrence with a four-step index
original.stem_html:
For non-negative integers \(n\), let

\[I_n=\int_{0}^{1} x^{n} e^{2 x^{4}}\,dx.\]
original.question_html:
For non-negative integers \(n\), let

\[I_n=\int_{0}^{1} x^{n} e^{2 x^{4}}\,dx.\]
(a)[2]

Evaluate \(I_3\) using \(u=2x^4\).

(b)[4]

For integers \(n\ge4\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-4}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n - 3} e^{2 x^{4}}\).

(c)[2]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{11}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The differential is \(du=8x^3\,dx\).

(b)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[- \frac{1}{8} + \frac{e^{2}}{8}\]

(b)

\[8 I_{n} + I_{n-4} \left(n - 3\right) = e^{2}\]

(c)

\[- \frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[I_3=\frac18\int_0^2e^u\,du=\frac{e^2-1}{8}.\]

(b)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n - 3} e^{2 x^{4}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=8 x^{3} x^{n - 3} e^{2 x^{4}} + \frac{x^{n - 3} \left(n - 3\right) e^{2 x^{4}}}{x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=8 x^{n} e^{2 x^{4}} + x^{n - 4} \left(n - 3\right) e^{2 x^{4}}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[8 I_{n} + I_{n-4} \left(n - 3\right) = e^{2}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(e^{2}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{3}=- \frac{1}{8} + \frac{e^{2}}{8}.\]
\[I_{7}=\frac{e^{2}-\left(4\right)\left(- \frac{1}{8} + \frac{e^{2}}{8}\right)}{8}=\frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}.\]
\[I_{11}=\frac{e^{2}-\left(8\right)\left(\frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}\right)}{8}=- \frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}.\]

original.title: Two integrations by parts with inverse powers
original.stem_html:
For positive integers \(n\), define

\[I_n=\int_1^2x^{-n}\sin\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx.\]
original.question_html:
For positive integers \(n\), define

\[I_n=\int_1^2x^{-n}\sin\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx.\]
(a)[5]

Prove the recurrence

\[n(n+1)I_{n+2}=n+\frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}}-\frac{\pi^2}{4}I_n.\]
(b)[2]

Express \(I_5\) in terms of \(I_1\) and \(\pi\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Track the sine and cosine values at both 1 and 2.

(b)

Apply the recurrence at n=1 and n=3.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[n(n+1)I_{n+2}=n+\frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}}-\frac{\pi^2}{4}I_n\]

(b)

\[I_5=\frac{\pi^{4} I_{1}}{384} - \frac{\pi^{2}}{96} - \frac{\pi^{3}}{384} + \frac{\pi}{192} + \frac{1}{4}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate \(I_{n+2}\) by parts, integrating the inverse power first:

\[I_{n+2}=\frac1{n+1}+\frac{\pi}{2(n+1)}\int_1^2x^{-n-1}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx.\]

A second integration by parts gives

\[\int_1^2x^{-n-1}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx=\frac{2^{-n}}n-\frac\pi{2n}I_n.\]

Substitute this into the first equation and multiply by \(n(n+1)\) to obtain the required identity.

(b)

\[2I_3=1+\frac\pi4-\frac{\pi^2}4I_1,\qquad 12I_5=3+\frac\pi{16}-\frac{\pi^2}4I_3.\]

Eliminating \(I_3\) gives

\[I_5=\frac{\pi^{4} I_{1}}{384} - \frac{\pi^{2}}{96} - \frac{\pi^{3}}{384} + \frac{\pi}{192} + \frac{1}{4}.\]

original.title: A weighted cosine family and volume
original.stem_html:
Define

\[I_n=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}e^{3x}\cos^n x\,dx\quad(n\ge0).\]
original.question_html:
Define

\[I_n=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}e^{3x}\cos^n x\,dx\quad(n\ge0).\]
(a)[3]

Evaluate \(I_0\) and show that \(I_1=\frac1{10}(e^{3\pi/2}+e^{-3\pi/2})\).

(b)[6]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive \((n^2+9)I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}\).

(c)[5]

The region under \(y=e^{3x/2}\cos^2x\) on \(-\pi/2\le x\le\pi/2\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the elementary antiderivative for an exponential times cosine.

(b)

The two boundary terms vanish only with the stated index restriction.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_0=- \frac{1}{3 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{3},\qquad I_1=\frac1{10}(e^{3\pi/2}+e^{-3\pi/2}).\]

(b)

\[(n^2+9)I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}\]

(c)

\[\frac{16 \pi \sinh{\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2} \right)}}{325}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The first is a direct exponential integral. For the second, two integrations by parts give

\[\int e^{3x}\cos x\,dx=\frac{e^{3x}}{10}(3\cos x+\sin x).\]

At the endpoints cosine is zero, giving

\[I_1=\frac1{10}(e^{3\pi/2}+e^{-3\pi/2}).\]

(b)

Write \(J=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} e^{3x}\sin x\cos^{n-1}x\,dx\). Integrating \(I_n\) by parts gives \(3I_n=nJ\) because the cosine-power boundary term vanishes. Integrate \(J\) by parts in the same way. Since \(n\ge2\), its boundary term also vanishes, and

\[3J=-I_n+(n-1)\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}e^{3x}\sin^2x\cos^{n-2}x\,dx.\]

Use \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\) and eliminate \(J\):

\[9I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}-n^2I_n.\]

Rearrangement proves the formula.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=- \frac{1}{3 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{3}.\]
\[I_{2}=- \frac{2}{39 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{2 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{39}.\]
\[I_{4}=- \frac{8}{325 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{8 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{325}.\]

Finally include the scale factor required by the application:

\[\piI_{4}=\frac{16 \pi \sinh{\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2} \right)}}{325}.\]

original.title: A hyperbolic recurrence with a boundary contribution
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_0^1(1-x)^n\sinh(2x)\,dx\) for non-negative integers \(n\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_0^1(1-x)^n\sinh(2x)\,dx\) for non-negative integers \(n\).

(a)[5]

Prove that \(4I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}-2\) for \(n\ge2\).

(b)[2]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The lower endpoint of cosh is 1, not 0.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[4I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}-2\]

(b)

\[-2 + \frac{3 \sinh^{2}{\left(1 \right)}}{2}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Integration by parts twice gives

\[I_n=-\frac12+\frac n2\int_0^1(1-x)^{n-1}\cosh(2x)\,dx.\]
\[\int_0^1(1-x)^{n-1}\cosh(2x)\,dx=\frac{n-1}2I_{n-2}.\]

The first lower boundary contributes \(-1/2\); both boundaries in the second integration are zero. Substitute and multiply by four.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=- \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\cosh{\left(2 \right)}}{2}.\]
\[I_{2}=- \frac{3}{4} + \frac{\cosh{\left(2 \right)}}{4}.\]
\[I_{4}=-2 + \frac{3 \sinh^{2}{\left(1 \right)}}{2}.\]

original.title: A quadratic-root family and a parabola
original.stem_html: For integer \(n\), define \(I_n=\int_0^4(9+x^2)^{n/2}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
For integer \(n\), define \(I_n=\int_0^4(9+x^2)^{n/2}\,dx\).

(a)[3]

Find \(I_{-1}\) in logarithmic form.

(b)[4]

For integers \(n\in\mathbb Z\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{n}{2}}\).

(c)[4]

The curve \(y=x^2/6\) is restricted to \(0\le x\le4\). Show that its length is \(I_1/3\) and evaluate that length exactly.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use a hyperbolic substitution.

(b)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\ln{\left(3 \right)}\]

(b)

\[I_{n} \left(n + 1\right) - 9 I_{n-2} n = 4 \cdot 5^{n}\]

(c)

\[\frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2} + \frac{10}{3}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Using \(x=3\sinh u\), the upper value of \(u\) is \(\sinh^{-1}(4/3)=\ln3\). The transformed integrand is 1, so \(I_{-1}=\ln3\).

(b)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{n}{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{n x^{2} \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{n}{2}}}{x^{2} + 9} + \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{n}{2}}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- 9 n \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{n}{2} - 1} + \left(n + 1\right) \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{n}{2}}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(n + 1\right) - 9 I_{n-2} n = 4 \cdot 5^{n}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(4 \cdot 5^{n}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(c)

The derivative is \(y^{\prime}=x/3\). Hence the speed is \(\sqrt{1+x^2/9}=\sqrt{9+x^2}/3\), so \(L=I_1/3\).

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{-1}=\ln{\left(3 \right)}.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{20-\left(-9\right)\left(\ln{\left(3 \right)}\right)}{2}=\frac{9 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2} + 10.\]

Finally include the scale factor required by the application:

\[\frac{1}{3}I_{1}=\frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2} + \frac{10}{3}.\]

original.title: Reducing powers of a cubic expression
original.stem_html: For non-negative integers \(n\), let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
For non-negative integers \(n\), let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n}\).

(b)[4]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(3 n + 1\right) - 6 I_{n-1} n = 3^{n}\]

(b)

\[\frac{837}{70}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{3 n x^{3} \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n}}{x^{3} + 2} + \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- 6 n \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n - 1} + \left(3 n + 1\right) \left(x^{3} + 2\right)^{n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(3 n + 1\right) - 6 I_{n-1} n = 3^{n}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(3^{n}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=1.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{3-\left(-6\right)\left(1\right)}{4}=\frac{9}{4}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{9-\left(-12\right)\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)}{7}=\frac{36}{7}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{27-\left(-18\right)\left(\frac{36}{7}\right)}{10}=\frac{837}{70}.\]

original.title: Mixed powers and a multiple-angle expansion
original.stem_html: Let \(J_{m,n}=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^m x\cos^n x\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Let \(J_{m,n}=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^m x\cos^n x\,dx\).

(a)[2]

Find \(\int\sin x\cos^n x\,dx\) for \(n\ne-1\).

(b)[5]

Show that \(J_{m,n}=\frac{m-1}{m+n}J_{m-2,n}\) for integers \(m\ge2,\ n\ge0\).

(c)[5]

By expanding \((z+z^{-1})^7\) with \(z=\cos x+i\sin x\), prove

\[64\cos^7x=\cos7x+7\cos5x+21\cos3x+35\cos x.\]
(d)[4]

Use these results to evaluate \(J_{4,7}\) exactly.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use cosine as the new variable.

(b)

Use a product whose values vanish at both ends.

(c)

Pair equal positive and negative powers of z.

(d)

First evaluate the pure cosine integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[-\frac{\cos^{n+1}x}{n+1}+C\]

(b)

\[J_{m,n}=\frac{m-1}{m+n}J_{m-2,n}\]

(c)

\[64\cos^7x=\cos7x+7\cos5x+21\cos3x+35\cos x\]

(d)

\[\frac{16}{1155}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\cos x\), so \(du=-\sin x\,dx\). Then the integral is \(-\int u^n\,du=-u^{n+1}/(n+1)+C\).

(b)

Differentiate \(\sin^{m-1}x\cos^{n+1}x\). Its derivative is

\[(m-1)\sin^{m-2}x\cos^{n+2}x-(n+1)\sin^m x\cos^n x.\]

Replace \(\cos^2x\) in the first term by \(1-\sin^2x\). Both endpoint values vanish, so integration yields

\[0=(m-1)J_{m-2,n}-(m+n)J_{m,n}.\]

(c)

Since \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos x\), the binomial expansion gives

\[128\cos^7x=(z^7+z^{-7})+7(z^5+z^{-5})+21(z^3+z^{-3})+35(z+z^{-1}).\]

De Moivre gives \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos(jx)\). Substitute and divide by two.

(d)

Integration of the cosine expansion gives

\[J_{0,7}=\frac1{64}\left(-\frac17+\frac75-7+35\right)=\frac{16}{35}.\]
\[J_{2,7}=\frac19J_{0,7},\qquad J_{4,7}=\frac3{11}J_{2,7}=\frac{16}{1155}.\]

\[I_{5}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9}-\left(-2\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12}\right)}{12}=\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{216}.\]

original.title: A polynomial-exponential boundary recurrence
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(2 x + 2\right)^{n} e^{- x}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(2 x + 2\right)^{n} e^{- x}\,dx\).

(a)[4]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(\left(2 x + 2\right)^{n} e^{- x}\).

(b)[2]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[- I_{n} + 2 I_{n-1} n = - 2^{n} + \frac{4^{n}}{e}\]

(b)

\[128 - \frac{304}{e}\]

(a)

Put \(H(x)=\left(2 x + 2\right)^{n} e^{- x}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2 n \left(2 x + 2\right)^{n} e^{- x}}{2 x + 2} - \left(2 x + 2\right)^{n} e^{- x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=2 n \left(2 x + 2\right)^{n - 1} e^{- x} - \left(2 x + 2\right)^{n} e^{- x}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[- I_{n} + 2 I_{n-1} n = - 2^{n} + \frac{4^{n}}{e}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(- 2^{n} + \frac{4^{n}}{e}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=1 - e^{-1}.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{-2 + \frac{4}{e}-\left(2\right)\left(1 - e^{-1}\right)}{-1}=4 - \frac{6}{e}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{-4 + \frac{16}{e}-\left(4\right)\left(4 - \frac{6}{e}\right)}{-1}=20 - \frac{40}{e}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{-8 + \frac{64}{e}-\left(6\right)\left(20 - \frac{40}{e}\right)}{-1}=128 - \frac{304}{e}.\]

original.title: A reciprocal hyperbolic-root reduction
original.stem_html: For positive integers \(n\), let \(I_n=\int_0^{12}(25+x^2)^{-n/2}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
For positive integers \(n\), let \(I_n=\int_0^{12}(25+x^2)^{-n/2}\,dx\).

(a)[3]

Find \(I_1\) in logarithmic form.

(b)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n+2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(x^{2} + 25\right)^{- \frac{n}{2}}\).

(c)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{5}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The pair 5,12 has hypotenuse 13.

(b)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\ln{\left(5 \right)}\]

(b)

\[I_{n} \left(1 - n\right) + 25 I_{n+2} n = 12 \cdot 13^{- n}\]

(c)

\[\frac{1452}{1373125}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[I_1=[\sinh^{-1}(x/5)]_0^{12}=\ln\left(\frac{12+13}{5}\right)=\ln5.\]

(b)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(x^{2} + 25\right)^{- \frac{n}{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{n x^{2} \left(x^{2} + 25\right)^{- \frac{n}{2}}}{x^{2} + 25} + \left(x^{2} + 25\right)^{- \frac{n}{2}}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=25 n \left(x^{2} + 25\right)^{- \frac{n}{2} - 1} + \left(1 - n\right) \left(x^{2} + 25\right)^{- \frac{n}{2}}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(1 - n\right) + 25 I_{n+2} n = 12 \cdot 13^{- n}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(12 \cdot 13^{- n}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{1}=\ln{\left(5 \right)}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{\frac{12}{13}-\left(0\right)\left(\ln{\left(5 \right)}\right)}{25}=\frac{12}{325}.\]
\[I_{5}=\frac{\frac{12}{2197}-\left(-2\right)\left(\frac{12}{325}\right)}{75}=\frac{1452}{1373125}.\]

original.title: A weighted hyperbolic reduction
original.stem_html: Set \(b=\ln(2+\sqrt3)\) and \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\ln{\left(\sqrt{3} + 2 \right)}} \tanh^{2}{\left(x \right)} \operatorname{sech}^{n}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).

Set \(b=\ln(2+\sqrt3)\) and \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\ln{\left(\sqrt{3} + 2 \right)}} \tanh^{2}{\left(x \right)} \operatorname{sech}^{n}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).

(a)[3]

(b)[2]

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\left(2 - n\right) \tanh^{2}{\left(x \right)} \operatorname{sech}^{n - 2}{\left(x \right)} + \left(n + 1\right) \tanh^{2}{\left(x \right)} \operatorname{sech}^{n}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(n + 1\right) + I_{n-2} \left(2 - n\right) = \tanh^{3}{\left(\ln{\left(\sqrt{3} + 2 \right)} \right)} \operatorname{sech}^{n - 2}{\left(\ln{\left(\sqrt{3} + 2 \right)} \right)}\]

\[I_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{8}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{32}-\left(-2\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{8}\right)}{5}=\frac{11 \sqrt{3}}{160}.\]
\[I_{6}=\frac{\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{128}-\left(-4\right)\left(\frac{11 \sqrt{3}}{160}\right)}{7}=\frac{191 \sqrt{3}}{4480}.\]

original.title: A secant substitution after reduction
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_2^{\sqrt5}(x^2-4)^n\,dx\) for non-negative integers \(n\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_2^{\sqrt5}(x^2-4)^n\,dx\) for non-negative integers \(n\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(x^{2} - 4\right)^{n}\).

(b)[4]

Use \(x=2\sec\theta\) to express \(I_n\) as a trigonometric integral, including its limits.

(c)[5]

Hence evaluate \(\int_0^{\tan^{-1}(1/2)}\frac{\sin^5\theta}{\cos^6\theta}\,d\theta\) exactly.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Find the angle using tangent, not the secant itself.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(2 n + 1\right) + 8 I_{n-1} n = \sqrt{5}\]

(b)

\[I_n=2^{2n+1}\int_0^{\tan^{-1}(1/2)}\tan^{2n+1}\theta\sec\theta\,d\theta.\]

(c)

\[- \frac{8}{15} + \frac{23 \sqrt{5}}{96}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(x^{2} - 4\right)^{n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2 n x^{2} \left(x^{2} - 4\right)^{n}}{x^{2} - 4} + \left(x^{2} - 4\right)^{n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=8 n \left(x^{2} - 4\right)^{n - 1} + \left(2 n + 1\right) \left(x^{2} - 4\right)^{n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(2 n + 1\right) + 8 I_{n-1} n = \sqrt{5}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(\sqrt{5}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The substitution gives \(x^2-4=4\tan^2\theta\) and \(dx=2\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\). At the upper limit \(\sec\theta=\sqrt5/2\), so \(\tan\theta=1/2\). Therefore the required expression follows.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=-2 + \sqrt{5}.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{5}-\left(8\right)\left(-2 + \sqrt{5}\right)}{3}=\frac{16}{3} - \frac{7 \sqrt{5}}{3}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{5}-\left(16\right)\left(\frac{16}{3} - \frac{7 \sqrt{5}}{3}\right)}{5}=- \frac{256}{15} + \frac{23 \sqrt{5}}{3}.\]

Finally include the scale factor required by the application:

\[\frac{1}{32}I_{2}=- \frac{8}{15} + \frac{23 \sqrt{5}}{96}.\]

original.question_html:
Define \(I_n=\int_0^{\pi/6}x^n\sin(3x)\,dx\).

(a)[5]

Show that for \(n\ge2\),

\[9I_n=n(\pi/6)^{n-1}-n(n-1)I_{n-2}.\]
(b)[2]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Each trigonometric integration produces a factor of one third.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[9I_n=n(\pi/6)^{n-1}-n(n-1)I_{n-2}\]

(b)

\[- \frac{2}{27} + \frac{\pi^{2}}{108}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate by parts, taking the trigonometric factor as the differential:

\[I_n=\frac n3\int_0^{\pi/6}x^{n-1}\cos(3x)\,dx.\]

Integrating this remaining integral by parts gives

\[I_n=\frac n9(\pi/6)^{n-1}-\frac{n(n-1)}9 I_{n-2}.\]

Multiplying by 9 proves the result.

(b)

Direct integration by parts gives I₁=1/9. Then use n=3:

\[I_{1}=\frac{1}{9}.\]
\[I_{3}=- \frac{2}{27} + \frac{\pi^{2}}{108}.\]

original.title: A rational quadratic reduction
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_0^3(9+x^2)^{-n}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n+1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{- n}\).

(b)[5]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(1 - 2 n\right) + 18 I_{n+1} n = 3 \cdot 18^{- n}\]

(b)

\[\frac{1}{972} + \frac{\pi}{2592}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{- n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{2 n x^{2} \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{- n}}{x^{2} + 9} + \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{- n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=18 n \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{- n - 1} + \left(1 - 2 n\right) \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{- n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(1 - 2 n\right) + 18 I_{n+1} n = 3 \cdot 18^{- n}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(3 \cdot 18^{- n}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The arctangent standard integral gives I₁=π/12. Apply the recurrence at n=1 and n=2:

\[I_{1}=\frac{\pi}{12}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{\frac{1}{6}-\left(-1\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)}{18}=\frac{1}{108} + \frac{\pi}{216}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{\frac{1}{108}-\left(-3\right)\left(\frac{1}{108} + \frac{\pi}{216}\right)}{36}=\frac{1}{972} + \frac{\pi}{2592}.\]

original.title: A fourth-power weight in a trigonometric family
original.stem_html: Define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^{n}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{4}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^{n}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{4}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).

(a)[2]

Find \(I_1\) by substitution.

(b)[5]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(\sin^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{5}{\left(x \right)}\).

(c)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{5}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Take cosine as the new variable.

(b)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{1}{5}\]

(b)

\[I_{n} \left(- n - 4\right) + I_{n-2} \left(n - 1\right) = 0\]

(c)

\[\frac{8}{315}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[I_1=-\int_1^0u^4\,du=\frac15,\qquad u=\cos x.\]

(b)

Put \(H(x)=\sin^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{5}{\left(x \right)}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{\left(n - 1\right) \sin^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{6}{\left(x \right)}}{\sin{\left(x \right)}} - 5 \sin{\left(x \right)} \sin^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{4}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\left(- n - 4\right) \sin^{n}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{4}{\left(x \right)} + \left(n - 1\right) \sin^{n - 2}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{4}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(- n - 4\right) + I_{n-2} \left(n - 1\right) = 0\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(0\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{1}=\frac{1}{5}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{0-\left(2\right)\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}{-7}=\frac{2}{35}.\]
\[I_{5}=\frac{0-\left(4\right)\left(\frac{2}{35}\right)}{-9}=\frac{8}{315}.\]

original.title: A telescoping family of trigonometric integrals
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \frac{\sin^{2 n}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos{\left(x \right)}}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \frac{\sin^{2 n}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos{\left(x \right)}}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

Show that \(I_n-I_{n+1}=\frac{2^{-(2n+1)}}{2n+1}\) for all non-negative integers \(n\).

(b)[5]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out the common sine power.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_n-I_{n+1}=\frac{2^{-(2n+1)}}{2n+1}\]

(b)

\[- \frac{263}{480} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Subtract the two integrands before integrating:

\[I_n-I_{n+1}=\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^{2n}x\cos x\,dx=\left[\frac{\sin^{2n+1}x}{2n+1}\right]_0^{\pi/6}.\]

Use \(\sin(\pi/6)=1/2\) to obtain the result.

(b)

The initial integral is I₀=[ln(sec x+tan x)]₀^(π/6)=½ ln3. Subtract the recurrence increments successively:

\[I_{0}=\frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}.\]
\[I_{1}=- \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}.\]
\[I_{2}=- \frac{13}{24} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}.\]
\[I_{3}=- \frac{263}{480} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}.\]

original.title: Eliminating a boundary term from a recurrence
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_1^{e^2}(\ln x)^n\,dx\).

(a)[5]

Derive \(I_n=2^ne^2-nI_{n-1}\) for \(n\ge1\).

(b)[3]

Eliminate \(e^2\) to obtain a relation involving \(I_n,I_{n-1},I_{n-2}\) for \(n\ge2\).

(c)[4]

Hence find the mean value of \((\ln x)^3\) on \(1\le x\le e^2\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The upper logarithm is 2, not 1.

(b)

Double the preceding-index equation.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_n=2^ne^2-nI_{n-1}\]

(b)

\[I_n=(2-n)I_{n-1}+2(n-1)I_{n-2}\]

(c)

\[- \frac{6 + 2 e^{2}}{1 - e^{2}}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Integration by parts with \(u=(\ln x)^n\) and \(dv=dx\) gives

\[I_n=[x(\ln x)^n]_1^{e^2}-n\int_1^{e^2}(\ln x)^{n-1}\,dx=2^ne^2-nI_{n-1}.\]

(b)

The preceding recurrence at index \(n-1\) gives

\[2^ne^2=2I_{n-1}+2(n-1)I_{n-2}.\]

Substitute into the formula for \(I_n\) and collect terms.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=-1 + e^{2}.\]
\[I_{1}=1 + e^{2}.\]
\[I_{2}=-2 + 2 e^{2}.\]
\[I_{3}=6 + 2 e^{2}.\]

Finally include the scale factor required by the application:

\[\frac{1}{-1 + e^{2}}I_{3}=- \frac{6 + 2 e^{2}}{1 - e^{2}}.\]

original.title: A recurrence from a sum-to-product identity
original.stem_html: Define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{\sin{\left(2 n x \right)}}{\cos{\left(x \right)}}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{\sin{\left(2 n x \right)}}{\cos{\left(x \right)}}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

Prove that for positive integers \(n\),

\[I_n+I_{n-1}=\frac{2[1-\cos((2n-1)\pi/3)]}{2n-1}.\]
(b)[4]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the numerator terms before cancelling cosine.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_n+I_{n-1}=\frac{2[1-\cos((2n-1)\pi/3)]}{2n-1}\]

(b)

\[\frac{29}{105}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Use the sum-to-product identity:

\[\sin(2nx)+\sin((2n-2)x)=2\sin((2n-1)x)\cos x.\]

Here \(\cos x\gt 0\) throughout the integration interval, so division is valid. Hence

\[I_n+I_{n-1}=2\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin((2n-1)x)\,dx.\]

Evaluate the cosine antiderivative to obtain the formula.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=0.\]
\[I_{1}=1.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{1}{3}.\]
\[I_{3}=- \frac{2}{15}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{29}{105}.\]

original.stem_html: For non-negative integers \(n\), let \(I_n=\int_0^\pi x^n\cos x\,dx\).
original.question_html:

original.title: Moments of a semicircular root
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_0^3 x^n\sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_0^3 x^n\sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n - 1} \left(9 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\).

(b)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{5}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(- n - 2\right) + I_{n-2} \left(9 n - 9\right) = 0\]

(b)

\[\frac{5832}{35}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n - 1} \left(9 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- 3 x x^{n - 1} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}} + \frac{x^{n - 1} \left(9 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \left(n - 1\right)}{x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=x^{n} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}} \left(- n - 2\right) + x^{n - 2} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}} \left(9 n - 9\right).\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(- n - 2\right) + I_{n-2} \left(9 n - 9\right) = 0\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(0\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The substitution u=9−x² gives I₁=9. Reduce the odd indices successively:

\[I_{1}=9.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{0-\left(18\right)\left(9\right)}{-5}=\frac{162}{5}.\]
\[I_{5}=\frac{0-\left(36\right)\left(\frac{162}{5}\right)}{-7}=\frac{5832}{35}.\]

original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^{4}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^{4}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(\sin^{5}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)}\).

(b)[4]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{6}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.

(a)

\[I_{n} \left(n + 4\right) + I_{n-2} \left(1 - n\right) = 0\]

(b)

\[\frac{3 \pi}{512}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=\sin^{5}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{\left(n - 1\right) \sin^{6}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos{\left(x \right)}} + 5 \sin^{4}{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\left(1 - n\right) \sin^{4}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n - 2}{\left(x \right)} + \left(n + 4\right) \sin^{4}{\left(x \right)} \cos^{n}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(n + 4\right) + I_{n-2} \left(1 - n\right) = 0\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(0\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Using sin²x=(1−cos2x)/2 twice gives I₀=3π/16. Apply the recurrence at n=2,4,6:

\[I_{0}=\frac{3 \pi}{16}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{0-\left(-1\right)\left(\frac{3 \pi}{16}\right)}{6}=\frac{\pi}{32}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{0-\left(-3\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{32}\right)}{8}=\frac{3 \pi}{256}.\]
\[I_{6}=\frac{0-\left(-5\right)\left(\frac{3 \pi}{256}\right)}{10}=\frac{3 \pi}{512}.\]

original.stem_html: For non-negative integers \(n\), define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \sec^{n}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
For non-negative integers \(n\), define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \sec^{n}{\left(x \right)}\,dx\).

(a)[2]

Find \(I_2\).

(b)[5]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec^{n - 2}{\left(x \right)}\).

(c)[4]

Find the volume formed by rotating the region under \(y=2\sec^2(2x)\) on \(0\le x\le\pi/12\) about the \(x\)-axis.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the derivative of tangent.

(b)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\]

(b)

\[I_{n} \left(n - 1\right) + I_{n-2} \left(2 - n\right) = 2^{n - 2} \cdot 3^{\frac{1}{2} - \frac{n}{2}}\]

(c)

\[\frac{20 \sqrt{3} \pi}{27}\]

(a)

\[I_2=[\tan x]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac1{\sqrt3}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\left(2 - n\right) \sec^{n - 2}{\left(x \right)} + \left(n - 1\right) \sec^{n}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(n - 1\right) + I_{n-2} \left(2 - n\right) = 2^{n - 2} \cdot 3^{\frac{1}{2} - \frac{n}{2}}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(2^{n - 2} \cdot 3^{\frac{1}{2} - \frac{n}{2}}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

\[I_{4}=\frac{\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{9}-\left(-2\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)}{3}=\frac{10 \sqrt{3}}{27}.\]

Finally include the scale factor required by the application:

\[2 \piI_{4}=\frac{20 \sqrt{3} \pi}{27}.\]

original.title: Bounding e squared using a positive integral
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}\,dx\).

(a)[4]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(\left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}\).

(b)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).

(c)[4]

Show that \(0\lt I_{4}\lt \frac{1}{3}\) and hence prove

\[7\lt e^{2}\lt \frac{67}{9}.\]
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.

(c)

Bound the integrand before isolating the exponential.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[2 I_{n} - I_{n-1} n = -1\]

(b)

\[- \frac{21}{4} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{4}\]

(c)

\[7\lt e^{2}\lt \frac{67}{9}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=\left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{n \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}}{1 - x} + 2 \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- n \left(1 - x\right)^{n - 1} e^{2 x} + 2 \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[2 I_{n} - I_{n-1} n = -1\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(-1\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=- \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{2}}{2}.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{-1-\left(-1\right)\left(- \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{2}}{2}\right)}{2}=- \frac{3}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{-1-\left(-2\right)\left(- \frac{3}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}\right)}{2}=- \frac{5}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{-1-\left(-3\right)\left(- \frac{5}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}\right)}{2}=- \frac{19}{8} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{8}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{-1-\left(-4\right)\left(- \frac{19}{8} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{8}\right)}{2}=- \frac{21}{4} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{4}.\]

(c)

For \(0\lt x\lt 1\), the function \(e^{2x}(1-x)^{2}\) is strictly decreasing from 1, because its logarithmic derivative is \(2-2/(1-x)\lt 0\). Thus

original.title: A non-square scale in a rational recurrence
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(2 x^{2} + 1\right)^{- n}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n+1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(2 x^{2} + 1\right)^{- n}\).

(b)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(1 - 2 n\right) + 2 I_{n+1} n = 3^{- n}\]

(b)

\[\frac{173}{1296} + \frac{5 \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{32}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(2 x^{2} + 1\right)^{- n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{4 n x^{2} \left(2 x^{2} + 1\right)^{- n}}{2 x^{2} + 1} + \left(2 x^{2} + 1\right)^{- n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=2 n \left(2 x^{2} + 1\right)^{- n - 1} + \left(1 - 2 n\right) \left(2 x^{2} + 1\right)^{- n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(1 - 2 n\right) + 2 I_{n+1} n = 3^{- n}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(3^{- n}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The initial integral follows from u=√2x: I₁=tan⁻¹(√2)/√2. Then:

\[I_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{2}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}-\left(-1\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{2}\right)}{2}=\frac{1}{6} + \frac{\sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{4}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{\frac{1}{9}-\left(-3\right)\left(\frac{1}{6} + \frac{\sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{4}\right)}{4}=\frac{11}{72} + \frac{3 \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{16}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{\frac{1}{27}-\left(-5\right)\left(\frac{11}{72} + \frac{3 \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{16}\right)}{6}=\frac{173}{1296} + \frac{5 \sqrt{2} \tan^{-1}{\left(\sqrt{2} \right)}}{32}.\]

original.title: Odd powers and a Gaussian factor
original.question_html:
Define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} x^{n} e^{- 3 x^{2}}\,dx\).

(a)[2]

Evaluate \(I_1\).

(b)[4]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n - 1} e^{- 3 x^{2}}\).

(c)

\[\frac{-13 + e^{3}}{27 e^{3}}\]

(a)

\[I_1=\left[-\frac16e^{-3x^2}\right]_0^1=\frac{1-e^{-3}}6.\]

(b)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n - 1} e^{- 3 x^{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- 6 x x^{n - 1} e^{- 3 x^{2}} + \frac{x^{n - 1} \left(n - 1\right) e^{- 3 x^{2}}}{x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- 6 x^{n} e^{- 3 x^{2}} + x^{n - 2} \left(n - 1\right) e^{- 3 x^{2}}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[- 6 I_{n} + I_{n-2} \left(n - 1\right) = e^{-3}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(e^{-3}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{1}=\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{6 e^{3}}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{e^{-3}-\left(2\right)\left(\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{6 e^{3}}\right)}{-6}=\frac{-4 + e^{3}}{18 e^{3}}.\]
\[I_{5}=\frac{e^{-3}-\left(4\right)\left(\frac{-4 + e^{3}}{18 e^{3}}\right)}{-6}=\frac{1}{27} - \frac{17}{54 e^{3}}.\]
\[I_{7}=\frac{e^{-3}-\left(6\right)\left(\frac{1}{27} - \frac{17}{54 e^{3}}\right)}{-6}=\frac{-13 + e^{3}}{27 e^{3}}.\]

original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^{n}}{\sqrt{9 - 5 x}}\,dx\).

(a)[4]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n} \sqrt{9 - 5 x}\).

(b)[3]

original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(- 5 n - \frac{5}{2}\right) + 9 I_{n-1} n = 2\]

(b)

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(- 5 n - \frac{5}{2}\right) + 9 I_{n-1} n = 2\]

(b)

\[I_{3}=\frac{2-\left(27\right)\left(\frac{92}{625}\right)}{- \frac{35}{2}}=\frac{2468}{21875}.\]

original.title: A reduction formula with rounded input
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n}\,dx\). It is given that \(I_1=0.79468444\) correct to 8 decimal places.
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n}\,dx\). It is given that \(I_1=0.79468444\) correct to 8 decimal places.

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n+1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n}\).

(b)[3]

Calculate \(I_3\) to 6 decimal places and give an upper bound for the error caused only by rounding \(I_1\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Eliminate I₂ to see how errors in I₁ are multiplied.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(1 - 4 n\right) + 4 I_{n+1} n = 3^{- n}\]

(b)

\(I_3\approx0.608317\); input-rounding error at most \(\frac{21}{6400000000}\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{8 n x^{4} \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n}}{2 x^{4} + 1} + \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=4 n \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n - 1} + \left(1 - 4 n\right) \left(2 x^{4} + 1\right)^{- n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(1 - 4 n\right) + 4 I_{n+1} n = 3^{- n}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(3^{- n}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

\[I_2=\frac{1/3+3I_1}{4},\qquad I_3=\frac{1/9+7I_2}{8}=\frac{25}{288}+\frac{21}{32}I_1.\]

Substitution gives \(0.6083172193055556\). The initial error is at most \(0.5\times10^{-8}\), so the induced error in \(I_3\) is at most \(\frac{21}{6400000000}\). This bound does not include the final displayed rounding.

original.title: A logarithmic recurrence with a polynomial weight
original.stem_html: Define \(I_n=\int_{1}^{e} x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Define \(I_n=\int_{1}^{e} x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{4} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}\).

(b)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[4 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = e^{4}\]

(b)

\[\frac{3}{128} + \frac{17 e^{4}}{128}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{4} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{n x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}}{\ln{\left(x \right)}} + 4 x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=n x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n - 1} + 4 x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[4 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = e^{4}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(e^{4}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=- \frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{4}}{4}.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{e^{4}-\left(1\right)\left(- \frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{4}}{4}\right)}{4}=\frac{1}{16} + \frac{3 e^{4}}{16}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{e^{4}-\left(2\right)\left(\frac{1}{16} + \frac{3 e^{4}}{16}\right)}{4}=- \frac{1}{32} + \frac{5 e^{4}}{32}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{e^{4}-\left(3\right)\left(- \frac{1}{32} + \frac{5 e^{4}}{32}\right)}{4}=\frac{3}{128} + \frac{17 e^{4}}{128}.\]

original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\cos^{2 n}{\left(x \right)}}{\sin{\left(x \right)}}\,dx\).
original.question_html:

(a)[5]

Prove \(I_n-I_{n+1}=\frac{(\sqrt3/2)^{2n+1}}{2n+1}\).

(b)[5]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).

(a)

Subtract before integrating and use u=cos x.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.

(a)

(b)

original.title: A three-halves root weight
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_0^1 x^n(1-x^2)^{3/2}\,dx\).

(a)[3]

Find \(\int x(1-x^2)^{3/2}\,dx\).

(b)[5]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n - 1} \left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}\).

(c)[3]

Use \(x=\sin u\) to evaluate \(I_0\).

(d)[2]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the expression inside the root as the variable.

(b)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(c)

Choose a branch on which cosine is nonnegative.

(d)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[-\frac15(1-x^2)^{5/2}+C\]

(b)

\[I_{n} \left(- n - 4\right) + I_{n-2} \left(n - 1\right) = 0\]

(c)

\[\frac{3 \pi}{16}\]

(d)

\[\frac{3 \pi}{256}\]

(a)

With \(u=1-x^2\), \(du=-2x\,dx\), so the integral is \(-\frac12\int u^{3/2}\,du=-u^{5/2}/5+C\).

(b)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n - 1} \left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- 5 x x^{n - 1} \left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} + \frac{x^{n - 1} \left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}} \left(n - 1\right)}{x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=x^{n} \left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \left(- n - 4\right) + x^{n - 2} \left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \left(n - 1\right).\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(- n - 4\right) + I_{n-2} \left(n - 1\right) = 0\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(0\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(c)

\[I_0=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^4u\,du=\frac18\int_0^{\pi/2}(3+4\cos2u+\cos4u)\,du=\frac{3\pi}{16}.\]

(d)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=\frac{3 \pi}{16}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{0-\left(1\right)\left(\frac{3 \pi}{16}\right)}{-6}=\frac{\pi}{32}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{0-\left(3\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{32}\right)}{-8}=\frac{3 \pi}{256}.\]

original.title: A recurrence and rational coefficients
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_1^{e^2}x^2(\ln x)^n\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}\).

(b)[4]

Prove by induction that \(I_n=A_ne^6+B_n\) for every non-negative integer \(n\), where \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are rational. State recurrences for these coefficients.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Track the coefficient of e⁶ separately from the constant term.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[3 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = 2^{n} e^{6}\]

(b)

\[A_0=\frac13,\quad B_0=-\frac13,\qquad A_n=\frac{2^n-nA_{n-1}}3,\quad B_n=-\frac n3B_{n-1}.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{n x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}}{\ln{\left(x \right)}} + 3 x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=n x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n - 1} + 3 x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[3 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = 2^{n} e^{6}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(2^{n} e^{6}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

For \(n=0\), direct integration gives \(I_0=(e^6-1)/3\), so the claim holds. Assume \(I_k=A_ke^6+B_k\) with rational coefficients. From the recurrence,

\[I_{k+1}=\frac{2^{k+1}e^6-(k+1)(A_ke^6+B_k)}3.\]

Thus \(A_{k+1}=[2^{k+1}-(k+1)A_k]/3\) and \(B_{k+1}=-(k+1)B_k/3\) are rational. This proves the next case, and hence all cases by induction.

original.title: A coth recurrence away from the pole
original.stem_html: Let \(I_n=\int_{\ln2}^{\ln3}\operatorname{coth}^n x\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{\ln2}^{\ln3}\operatorname{coth}^n x\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(\coth^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)}\).

(b)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{6}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(1 - n\right) + I_{n-2} \left(n - 1\right) = - \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^{n - 1} + \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^{n - 1}\]

(b)

\[- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \frac{813805}{248832}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=\coth^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{\left(n - 1\right) \coth^{n - 1}{\left(x \right)}}{\sinh^{2}{\left(x \right)} \coth{\left(x \right)}}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\left(1 - n\right) \coth^{n}{\left(x \right)} + \left(n - 1\right) \coth^{n - 2}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(1 - n\right) + I_{n-2} \left(n - 1\right) = - \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^{n - 1} + \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^{n - 1}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(- \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^{n - 1} + \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^{n - 1}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The initial integral is I₀=ln(3/2), while coth(ln2)=5/3 and coth(ln3)=5/4. Successive substitution gives:

\[I_{0}=- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{- \frac{5}{12}-\left(1\right)\left(- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \ln{\left(3 \right)}\right)}{-1}=- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \frac{5}{12} + \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{- \frac{4625}{1728}-\left(3\right)\left(- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \frac{5}{12} + \ln{\left(3 \right)}\right)}{-3}=- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \frac{6785}{5184}.\]
\[I_{6}=\frac{- \frac{2440625}{248832}-\left(5\right)\left(- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \frac{6785}{5184}\right)}{-5}=- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \frac{813805}{248832}.\]

original.title: A polynomial and an endpoint root
original.stem_html: Define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{2} x^{n} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
Define \(I_n=\int_{0}^{2} x^{n} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}\).

(b)[3]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(- n - \frac{5}{2}\right) + 2 I_{n-1} n = 0\]

(b)

\[\frac{1024 \sqrt{2}}{1155}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{n x^{n} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{x} - \frac{5 x^{n} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=2 n x^{n - 1} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} + x^{n} \left(2 - x\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \left(- n - \frac{5}{2}\right).\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(- n - \frac{5}{2}\right) + 2 I_{n-1} n = 0\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(0\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=\frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{5}.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{0-\left(2\right)\left(\frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{5}\right)}{- \frac{7}{2}}=\frac{32 \sqrt{2}}{35}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{0-\left(4\right)\left(\frac{32 \sqrt{2}}{35}\right)}{- \frac{9}{2}}=\frac{256 \sqrt{2}}{315}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{0-\left(6\right)\left(\frac{256 \sqrt{2}}{315}\right)}{- \frac{11}{2}}=\frac{1024 \sqrt{2}}{1155}.\]

original.title: A quartic-expression recurrence
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(x^{4} + 3\right)^{n}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(x^{4} + 3\right)^{n}\).

(b)[4]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_{n} \left(4 n + 1\right) - 12 I_{n-1} n = 4^{n}\]

(b)

\[\frac{2176}{65}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x \left(x^{4} + 3\right)^{n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{4 n x^{4} \left(x^{4} + 3\right)^{n}}{x^{4} + 3} + \left(x^{4} + 3\right)^{n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- 12 n \left(x^{4} + 3\right)^{n - 1} + \left(4 n + 1\right) \left(x^{4} + 3\right)^{n}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(4 n + 1\right) - 12 I_{n-1} n = 4^{n}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(4^{n}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=1.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{4-\left(-12\right)\left(1\right)}{5}=\frac{16}{5}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{16-\left(-24\right)\left(\frac{16}{5}\right)}{9}=\frac{464}{45}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{64-\left(-36\right)\left(\frac{464}{45}\right)}{13}=\frac{2176}{65}.\]

original.title: A factorial bound for exponential moments
original.stem_html: For non-negative integers \(n\), let \(I_n=\int_0^2x^ne^{-2x}\,dx\).
original.question_html:
For non-negative integers \(n\), let \(I_n=\int_0^2x^ne^{-2x}\,dx\).

(a)[4]

For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n} e^{- 2 x}\).

(b)[4]

Prove by induction that \(0\lt I_n\lt \frac{n!}{2^{n+1}}\) for every non-negative integer \(n\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

The subtracted boundary term makes the inequality strict.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[- 2 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = \frac{2^{n}}{e^{4}}\]

(b)

\[0\lt I_n\lt \frac{n!}{2^{n+1}}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n} e^{- 2 x}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{n x^{n} e^{- 2 x}}{x} - 2 x^{n} e^{- 2 x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=n x^{n - 1} e^{- 2 x} - 2 x^{n} e^{- 2 x}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[- 2 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = \frac{2^{n}}{e^{4}}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(\frac{2^{n}}{e^{4}}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The integrand is positive on the interior, so \(I_n\gt 0\). Also \(I_0=(1-e^{-4})/2\lt 1/2\). Suppose \(I_k\lt k!/2^{k+1}\). The recurrence gives

\[I_{k+1}=\frac{k+1}{2}I_k-2^ke^{-4}\lt \frac{k+1}{2}\frac{k!}{2^{k+1}}=\frac{(k+1)!}{2^{k+2}}.\]

Thus the claim holds at the next index; induction proves it for all non-negative integers.

original.title: A truncated circular-root family
original.question_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{x^{n}}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}}\,dx\).

(a)[5]

For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n - 1} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}}\).

(b)[4]

Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[- I_{n} n + I_{n-2} \left(9 n - 9\right) = 2^{- n} 3^{n + \frac{1}{2}}\]

(b)

\[- \frac{567 \sqrt{3}}{64} + \frac{81 \pi}{16}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n - 1} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{x x^{n - 1}}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}} + \frac{x^{n - 1} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}} \left(n - 1\right)}{x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{n x^{n}}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}} + \frac{x^{n - 2} \left(9 n - 9\right)}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[- I_{n} n + I_{n-2} \left(9 n - 9\right) = 2^{- n} 3^{n + \frac{1}{2}}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(2^{- n} 3^{n + \frac{1}{2}}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The initial value is I₀=[sin⁻¹(x/3)]₀^(3/2)=π/6. Keep the nonzero upper boundary term when reducing:

\[I_{0}=\frac{\pi}{6}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{\frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{4}-\left(9\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)}{-2}=- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{8} + \frac{3 \pi}{4}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{\frac{81 \sqrt{3}}{16}-\left(27\right)\left(- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{8} + \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)}{-4}=- \frac{567 \sqrt{3}}{64} + \frac{81 \pi}{16}.\]

original.title: A hyperbolic parametrisation of a circular surface
original.stem_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad y=3 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}.\]
original.question_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad y=3 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}.\]
(a)[4]

Show that \(ds/dt=6\operatorname{sech}(2t)\) and set up the surface integral about the \(x\)-axis.

(b)[4]

Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity.

(b)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[S=36\pi\int_0^{(\ln2)/2}\tanh(2t)\operatorname{sech}(2t)\,dt\]

(b)

\[\frac{18 \pi}{5}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[x^{\prime}=-6\operatorname{sech}(2t)\tanh(2t),\qquad y^{\prime}=6\operatorname{sech}^2(2t).\]

Using \(\tanh^2v+\operatorname{sech}^2v=1\), the squared speed is \(36\operatorname{sech}^2(2t)\). Both the speed and radius are nonnegative, giving the stated integral.

(b)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}}\left(3 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=- 6 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)} \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=6 - 6 \tanh^{2}{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=6 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(18 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)} \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}\right)\,dt=- 9 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[- 9 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}}=\frac{18 \pi}{5}.\]

original.stem_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=- 4 t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2},\qquad y=4 e^{t},\qquad 0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]
original.question_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=- 4 t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2},\qquad y=4 e^{t},\qquad 0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]
(a)[5]

Find the exact length of the specified arc.

(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{3}{2} + 4 \ln{\left(2 \right)}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=e^{2 t} - 4,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=4 e^{t}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\left(e^{2 t} + 4\right)^{2}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}e^{2 t} + 4\,dt=\left[4 t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2}\right]_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}=\frac{3}{2} + 4 \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]

original.stem_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 t - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=3 - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)},\qquad 0\le t\le \pi.\]
original.question_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 t - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=3 - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)},\qquad 0\le t\le \pi.\]
(a)[4]

Show that the surface area about the \(x\)-axis can be written as \(72\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^3(t/2)\,dt\).

(b)[4]

Evaluate this surface area exactly.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Rewrite 1−cos t using the half-angle.

(b)

Integrate sin u(1−cos²u).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[S=72\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^3(t/2)\,dt\]

(b)

\[96 \pi\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[(x^{\prime})^2+(y^{\prime})^2=9(1-\cos t)^2+9\sin^2t=36\sin^2(t/2).\]

On \(0\le t\le\pi\), sine of the half-angle is nonnegative. Since \(y=6\sin^2(t/2)\), multiplying the radius, speed and \(2\pi\) gives the required integral.

(b)

Put \(u=t/2\). Then

\[\int_0^\pi\sin^3(t/2)\,dt=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin u(1-\cos^2u)\,du=\frac43.\]
\[S=72\pi\cdot\frac43=96\pi.\]

original.stem_html:

original.question_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=4 t + 3 \cosh{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=- 3 t + 4 \cosh{\left(t \right)},\qquad -1\le t\le 1.\]
(a)[4]

Show that \(ds/dt=5\cosh t\).

(b)[4]

Explain why the radius for rotation about the \(y\)-axis is \(x\) throughout the arc, and show that the surface area is \(30\pi\int_{-1}^1\cosh^2t\,dt\).

The cross terms cancel on expansion.

(b)

original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{ds}{dt}=5\cosh t\]

(b)

\[S=30\pi\int_{-1}^1\cosh^2t\,dt\]

(c)

\[S=30\pi+\frac{15\pi}{2}(e^2-e^{-2})\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[(3\sinh t+4)^2+(4\sinh t-3)^2=25(1+\sinh^2t)=25\cosh^2t.\]

Since \(\cosh t\gt 0\), take the positive root.

(b)

On this interval, \(x^{\prime}=3\sinh t+4\ge4-3\sinh1\gt 0\), since \(\sinh1\approx1.1752\). The minimum radius occurs at t=−1, where \(x(-1)=3\cosh1-4\approx0.6292\gt 0\). Therefore x is positive throughout. The surface integral is

The \(t\cosh t\) term is odd and integrates to zero.

(c)

\[\int_{-1}^1\cosh^2t\,dt=\left[\frac t2+\frac14\sinh2t\right]_{-1}^1=1+\frac12\sinh2.\]

Therefore

\[S=30\pi+15\pi\sinh2=30\pi+\frac{15\pi}{2}(e^2-e^{-2}).\]

original.title: An intersection that determines an arc endpoint
original.stem_html: The curves \(C_1:y=2\cosh(x/2)\) and \(C_2:y=3\sinh x\) are considered for real \(x\).
original.question_html:
The curves \(C_1:y=2\cosh(x/2)\) and \(C_2:y=3\sinh x\) are considered for real \(x\).

(a)[4]

Show that they intersect at a unique point with \(x=a=2\ln\frac{1+\sqrt{10}}3\).

(b)[3]

Sketch both curves on the same axes, indicating the intercepts and their intersection.

(c)[4]

Find the exact length of \(C_1\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=a\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the double-angle identity and do not divide by sinh.

(b)

Use symmetry and the fact that the intersection is unique.

(c)

The speed is cosh(x/2), and the endpoint sinh is already known.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=2\ln\frac{1+\sqrt{10}}3\]

(b)

The intercepts are \((0,2)\) and \((0,0)\); the intersection is \((a,2\sqrt{10}/3)\).

(c)

\[\frac{2}{3}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(\sinh x=2\sinh(x/2)\cosh(x/2)\), the intersection equation becomes

\[2\cosh(x/2)=6\sinh(x/2)\cosh(x/2).\]

Divide by the strictly positive cosh factor: \(\sinh(x/2)=1/3\). The sinh function is strictly increasing, so the solution is unique, and its inverse logarithmic form gives the stated value.

(b)

The cosh curve is even with minimum \((0,2)\). The sinh curve is odd and strictly increasing through the origin. It is below the first curve for \(x\lt a\) and above it for \(x\gt a\). Mark the unique intersection \((a,2\sqrt{10}/3)\).

(c)

Here \(y^{\prime}=\sinh(x/2)\), so \(\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}=\cosh(x/2)\). Thus

\[L=\int_0^a\cosh(x/2)\,dx=2\sinh(a/2)=\frac23.\]

The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=- t^{2} + 8 t,\qquad y=\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3},\qquad 0\le t\le 2.\]

For derivative calculations use \(0\lt t\lt 2\); endpoint values are interpreted by limits.

(a)[5]

Find \(dy/dx\) and \(d^2y/dx^2\) in terms of \(t\).

(b)[3]

Find the mean value of \(d^2y/dx^2\) with respect to \(x\) over the whole arc.

(c)[6]

Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The second derivative requires another division by dx/dt.

(b)

Integrate the derivative via its endpoint values.

(c)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{4 \sqrt{t}}{t - 4},\qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{- t - 4}{\sqrt{t} \left(t - 4\right)^{3}}\]

(b)

\[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\]

(c)

\[\frac{19456 \sqrt{2} \pi}{105}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

First divide the parameter derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{8\sqrt t}{8-2t}=\frac{4\sqrt t}{4-t}.\]

Differentiate this ratio with respect to \(t\) and divide again by \(dx/dt=8-2t\). This gives

\[\frac{- t - 4}{\sqrt{t} \left(t - 4\right)^{3}}\]

(b)

The average of the second derivative is the endpoint change in the first derivative divided by the interval length:

\[\text{mean}=\frac{[dy/dx]_{t=0}^{t=2}}{x(2)-x(0)}=\frac{2\sqrt2-0}{12}=\frac{\sqrt2}{6}.\]

(c)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{2}\left(\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

original.title: A cardioid: area, length and an arc bisector
original.stem_html: Let \(a\gt 0\). A polar curve is given by \(r=a(1+\cos\theta)\) for \(-\pi\le\theta\le\pi\).
original.question_html:
Let \(a\gt 0\). A polar curve is given by \(r=a(1+\cos\theta)\) for \(-\pi\le\theta\le\pi\).

(a)[3]

Sketch the curve and state its maximum distance from the pole.

(b)[3]

Find its enclosed area.

(c)[4]

Find the length of the upper half of the curve, from \(\theta=0\) to \(\theta=\pi\).

(d)[3]

Find the angle \(\alpha\) which bisects this upper-half arc by length, measured from \(\theta=0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use symmetry and the values at multiples of π/2.

(b)

Use the polar area formula and symmetry.

(c)

Choose the nonnegative half-angle square root.

(d)

Half the arc length is not generally half the angle.
original.answer_html:
(a)

A right-facing cardioid, symmetric about the initial line; maximum radius \(2a\).

(b)

\[\frac32\pi a^2\]

(c)

\[4a\]

(d)

\[\alpha=\frac\pi3\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The pole occurs at \(\theta=\pm\pi\). The largest radius is \(2a\) at \(\theta=0\). The points at \(\theta=\pm\pi/2\) have radius \(a\). These features determine the sketch.

(b)

\[A=\frac12\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}a^2(1+\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac12a^2(2\pi+0+\pi)=\frac32\pi a^2.\]

(c)

\[\sqrt{r^2+(dr/d\theta)^2}=a\sqrt{2+2\cos\theta}=2a\cos(\theta/2).\]

The cosine is nonnegative on this interval. Therefore

\[L=2a\int_0^\pi\cos(\theta/2)\,d\theta=4a.\]

(d)

\[2a\int_0^\alpha\cos(\theta/2)\,d\theta=2a\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sin(\alpha/2)=\frac12.\]

Because \(0\le\alpha\le\pi\), the unique solution is \(\alpha=\pi/3\).
